questions.question: What does selectively permeable mean when describing the cell membrane?
options: Some substances cross more readily than others
Every substance crosses at the same rate
Nothing can ever cross the membrane
Only water is allowed to leave the cell
questions.explanation: Selective permeability gives the cell different levels of control over different substances. Equating selective permeability with complete permeability removes the membrane’s regulatory role.
questions.sourceEvidence: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that regulates the passage of substances into and out of the cell, maintaining internal homeostasis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Equating selective permeability with complete permeability removes the membrane’s regulatory role

questions.question: Why is the phospholipid bilayer essential for homeostasis?
options: It makes the cytoplasm chemically identical to the environment
It regulates movement into and out of the cell
It produces all cellular proteins
It permanently fixes the cell volume
questions.explanation: Controlled exchange helps preserve stable internal conditions. Assuming homeostasis requires no exchange confuses regulation with isolation.
questions.sourceEvidence: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that regulates the passage of substances into and out of the cell, maintaining internal homeostasis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming homeostasis requires no exchange confuses regulation with isolation

questions.question: Which structural description best identifies the cell membrane?
options: A freely permeable protein monolayer
A rigid wall made only of cellulose
A selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer
A double layer of nucleic acids
questions.explanation: The membrane consists principally of two phospholipid layers with selective permeability. Calling it a protein monolayer omits the bilayer that forms the barrier.
questions.sourceEvidence: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that regulates the passage of substances into and out of the cell, maintaining internal homeostasis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling it a protein monolayer omits the bilayer that forms the barrier

questions.question: What boundary does the cell membrane establish?
options: A boundary between DNA and RNA within a gene
A boundary between two chromosomes
A boundary separating every enzyme from its substrate
A boundary between cytoplasm and the external environment
questions.explanation: The membrane encloses the cytoplasm and distinguishes the cell interior from its surroundings. Placing the boundary inside a gene confuses cell organization with genetic structure.
questions.sourceEvidence: By separating the cytoplasm from the external environment, it lets the cell control ion concentrations, nutrient uptake, waste removal, electrical signalling, and communication with other cells.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Placing the boundary inside a gene confuses cell organization with genetic structure

questions.question: If a membrane suddenly became freely permeable to ions, which function would fail first?
options: Control of internal ion concentrations
Storage of nucleotide sequence
Formation of peptide bonds by ribosomes
Replication of chromosomes only
questions.explanation: The membrane maintains controlled ion concentrations by regulating passage. Assuming ions can equilibrate freely while homeostasis remains unchanged ignores the selective barrier.
questions.sourceEvidence: By separating the cytoplasm from the external environment, it lets the cell control ion concentrations, nutrient uptake, waste removal, electrical signalling, and communication with other cells.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming ions can equilibrate freely while homeostasis remains unchanged ignores the selective barrier

questions.question: Which set of processes is directly regulated by the cell membrane?
options: DNA replication, transcription, and chromosome pairing
Nutrient uptake, waste removal, and ion balance
Only protein folding and enzyme synthesis
Bone growth, blood clotting, and digestion exclusively
questions.explanation: Membrane transport governs nutrients, wastes, and ions crossing the cell boundary. Assigning nuclear information processing to the membrane confuses transport with gene expression.
questions.sourceEvidence: By separating the cytoplasm from the external environment, it lets the cell control ion concentrations, nutrient uptake, waste removal, electrical signalling, and communication with other cells.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning nuclear information processing to the membrane confuses transport with gene expression

questions.question: How does the membrane contribute to communication between cells?
options: It merges the cytoplasm of all neighboring cells
It converts every receptor into DNA
It controls interactions and signals across the cell boundary
It prevents any external molecule from approaching
questions.explanation: A regulated boundary allows the cell to receive and send signals while remaining distinct. Complete isolation would prevent the communication that the membrane helps coordinate.
questions.sourceEvidence: By separating the cytoplasm from the external environment, it lets the cell control ion concentrations, nutrient uptake, waste removal, electrical signalling, and communication with other cells.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Complete isolation would prevent the communication that the membrane helps coordinate

questions.question: A cell maintains a stable interior while its surroundings change. Which membrane property makes this possible?
options: Unrestricted diffusion of every solute
Permanent closure of all transport proteins
Replacement of cytoplasm with extracellular fluid
Selective control of substance passage
questions.explanation: Selective passage lets the cell respond to its environment without simply matching it. Unrestricted equilibration would erase the internal conditions required for homeostasis.
questions.sourceEvidence: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that regulates the passage of substances into and out of the cell, maintaining internal homeostasis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Unrestricted equilibration would erase the internal conditions required for homeostasis

questions.question: Why is a phospholipid described as amphipathic?
options: It has a water-attracting head and water-avoiding tails
Both its head and tails avoid water
It is composed entirely of charged protein
It can move only through aquaporins
questions.explanation: A phospholipid combines hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions in one molecule. Calling the entire molecule hydrophobic ignores the phosphate head’s interaction with water.
questions.sourceEvidence: Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules: each has a hydrophilic phosphate head that interacts with water and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails that avoid water.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling the entire molecule hydrophobic ignores the phosphate head’s interaction with water

questions.question: How do phospholipids orient themselves in a watery environment?
options: Tails face water while heads cluster inside
Heads face water while tails point inward toward one another
Heads and tails alternate randomly across one layer
Every phospholipid leaves the water completely
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic heads contact cytoplasmic or extracellular water while hydrophobic tails are sheltered inside. Reversing the orientation would expose fatty-acid tails to water.
questions.sourceEvidence: In a watery environment they self-assemble into two layers, with heads facing the cytoplasm and extracellular fluid while tails point inward.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the orientation would expose fatty-acid tails to water

questions.question: What most directly causes phospholipids to form a bilayer spontaneously?
options: ATP pumps each phospholipid into a fixed position
Ribosomes assemble the membrane one molecule at a time
Their hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions interact differently with water
Sodium ions covalently link every phosphate head
questions.explanation: Amphipathic behavior drives heads toward water and tails away from it. Requiring ATP for bilayer self-assembly overlooks the physical behavior of amphipathic molecules.
questions.sourceEvidence: In a watery environment they self-assemble into two layers, with heads facing the cytoplasm and extracellular fluid while tails point inward.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Requiring ATP for bilayer self-assembly overlooks the physical behavior of amphipathic molecules

questions.question: What is cholesterol’s main role within the bilayer?
options: It translates mRNA into protein
It pumps three sodium ions outward
It forms the cell’s genetic code
It buffers membrane fluidity
questions.explanation: Cholesterol between phospholipids helps stabilize how fluid the membrane is. Treating cholesterol as a transport pump confuses a lipid component with a membrane protein.
questions.sourceEvidence: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids and buffers fluidity, while membrane proteins provide channels, carriers, receptors, enzymes, and attachment points.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating cholesterol as a transport pump confuses a lipid component with a membrane protein

questions.question: Which membrane component can act as a channel, carrier, receptor, or enzyme?
options: Membrane protein
Fatty-acid tail
Cholesterol molecule only
Cytoplasmic glucose molecule
questions.explanation: Embedded proteins provide specialized transport, signaling, catalytic, and attachment functions. Assigning all specialized functions to phospholipid tails ignores the roles of membrane proteins.
questions.sourceEvidence: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids and buffers fluidity, while membrane proteins provide channels, carriers, receptors, enzymes, and attachment points.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning all specialized functions to phospholipid tails ignores the roles of membrane proteins

questions.question: Why would loss of the membrane disrupt enzyme-controlled metabolism?
options: All enzymes would immediately become DNA
The cell could no longer maintain the required internal chemical environment
Substrates would stop having molecular motion
The nucleus would become the extracellular fluid
questions.explanation: Cellular enzymes depend on controlled internal chemical conditions. Assuming enzymes work identically in any environment ignores their dependence on cellular homeostasis.
questions.sourceEvidence: Without a membrane, a cell could not maintain the specific internal chemical environment required for its enzymes and metabolic reactions to function.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming enzymes work identically in any environment ignores their dependence on cellular homeostasis

questions.question: Why must cells maintain Na⁺, K⁺, and Ca²⁺ gradients?
options: The gradients make every transport process passive
The gradients eliminate the need for membranes
The gradients support signaling, protein function, and energy production
The gradients convert lipids into chromosomes
questions.explanation: Ion gradients provide stored electrochemical differences used in essential cellular processes. Treating ion gradients as irrelevant overlooks their roles in electrical and metabolic work.
questions.sourceEvidence: Concentration gradients of ions like Na⁺, K⁺, and Ca²⁺ are essential for electrical signaling, protein function, and energy production.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating ion gradients as irrelevant overlooks their roles in electrical and metabolic work

questions.question: What would happen to internal solute concentrations if the membrane became freely permeable?
options: They would remain permanently unchanged
Every solute would become more concentrated inside
Only DNA would diffuse out while ions stayed fixed
They would rapidly approach the concentrations outside the cell
questions.explanation: Free permeability allows concentration differences to dissipate toward equilibrium. Claiming gradients persist without a selective barrier ignores diffusion down concentration gradients.
questions.sourceEvidence: A freely permeable cell would rapidly equilibrate with its external environment, losing the controlled concentrations that make life possible.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Claiming gradients persist without a selective barrier ignores diffusion down concentration gradients

questions.question: What two features define passive transport?
options: Movement down a gradient without ATP
Movement against a gradient using ATP
Vesicle fusion driven by ATP
Random movement that always increases a gradient
questions.explanation: Passive transport follows an existing concentration or electrochemical gradient and needs no ATP input. Calling movement against a gradient passive reverses the energetic definition.
questions.sourceEvidence: Passive transport moves substances down their concentration or electrochemical gradient and requires no ATP.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling movement against a gradient passive reverses the energetic definition

questions.question: A small non-polar gas crosses directly through the lipid bilayer. Which process is occurring?
options: Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion
Active transport
Endocytosis
questions.explanation: Small non-polar molecules can pass through the bilayer by simple diffusion. Requiring a carrier for every molecule ignores direct diffusion through lipids.
questions.sourceEvidence: Small non-polar molecules cross by simple diffusion; polar molecules and ions use channel or carrier proteins in facilitated diffusion.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Requiring a carrier for every molecule ignores direct diffusion through lipids

questions.question: An ion moves down its electrochemical gradient through a channel protein. How should this be classified?
options: Primary active transport
Osmosis
Facilitated diffusion
Exocytosis
questions.explanation: The ion moves passively but receives help from a membrane protein. Calling all protein-assisted movement active incorrectly treats the presence of a protein as proof of ATP use.
questions.sourceEvidence: Small non-polar molecules cross by simple diffusion; polar molecules and ions use channel or carrier proteins in facilitated diffusion.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling all protein-assisted movement active incorrectly treats the presence of a protein as proof of ATP use

questions.question: Across a selectively permeable membrane, which direction does water move by osmosis?
options: Toward the side with lower solute concentration
Only toward the side with more ATP
In no direction unless solute crosses first
Toward the side with higher solute concentration
questions.explanation: Water moves from lower solute concentration toward higher solute concentration. Following the solute gradient in the wrong direction reverses osmotic water movement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Osmosis is the passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, often through aquaporins, from lower solute concentration toward higher solute concentration.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Following the solute gradient in the wrong direction reverses osmotic water movement

questions.question: An animal cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. What net water movement is expected?
options: Water enters the cell
Water leaves the cell
No water crosses the membrane
Only solute leaves through aquaporins
questions.explanation: The lower external solute concentration drives water toward the more concentrated cell interior. Predicting water loss from a hypotonic solution reverses the osmotic gradient.
questions.sourceEvidence: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell's interior.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Predicting water loss from a hypotonic solution reverses the osmotic gradient

questions.question: Why can a red blood cell rupture in distilled water?
options: ATP pumps all water into the nucleus
Osmotic water entry causes swelling without a rigid wall
The bilayer becomes a cellulose wall
Sodium leaves and removes all internal water
questions.explanation: Distilled water is strongly hypotonic, so continued water entry can produce osmotic lysis. Blaming rupture on water leaving the cell predicts shrinkage rather than swelling.
questions.sourceEvidence: In animal cells without rigid walls, this can continue until the membrane ruptures — a process called cytolysis or osmotic lysis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Blaming rupture on water leaving the cell predicts shrinkage rather than swelling

questions.question: Why does a plant cell resist bursting better than an animal cell in a hypotonic solution?
options: Its membrane is freely permeable to every solute
Its aquaporins pump water outward using ATP
Its cell wall generates opposing turgor pressure
Its cytoplasm contains no dissolved substances
questions.explanation: The rigid wall resists expansion and builds pressure against further water entry. Attributing protection to the absence of osmosis ignores that water still enters plant cells.
questions.sourceEvidence: Plant cells resist this because their cell wall provides a rigid structure that creates turgor pressure, opposing further water entry.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing protection to the absence of osmosis ignores that water still enters plant cells

questions.question: What role do aquaporins play in osmosis?
options: They hydrolyze ATP to move solutes uphill
They convert water into sodium ions
They block all water from crossing
They provide membrane pathways for passive water movement
questions.explanation: Aquaporins facilitate water passage while osmosis remains passive. Calling aquaporins ATP pumps confuses facilitated water movement with active transport.
questions.sourceEvidence: Osmosis is the passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, often through aquaporins, from lower solute concentration toward higher solute concentration.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling aquaporins ATP pumps confuses facilitated water movement with active transport

questions.question: When is membrane transport classified as active?
options: When a substance moves against its gradient using energy
When water moves toward higher solute concentration without ATP
When a gas diffuses through the bilayer
When an ion moves down its gradient through a channel
questions.explanation: Active transport couples energy use to movement against a concentration gradient. Calling all membrane movement active ignores both direction and energy source.
questions.sourceEvidence: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and therefore requires energy.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling all membrane movement active ignores both direction and energy source

questions.question: What binds to the Na⁺/K⁺ pump at the start of its cycle on the cytoplasmic side?
options: Two K⁺ ions and no ATP
Three Na⁺ ions and ATP
Three K⁺ ions and glucose
One Na⁺ ion and two proteins
questions.explanation: The inward-facing pump initially binds three cytoplasmic sodium ions plus ATP. Starting with extracellular potassium skips the sodium-binding state.
questions.sourceEvidence: In its first state, it binds 3 Na⁺ ions from the cytoplasm and one ATP molecule.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Starting with extracellular potassium skips the sodium-binding state

questions.question: What directly causes the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to expose its Na⁺ sites to the outside?
options: Osmosis pulls the protein through the bilayer
K⁺ diffusion removes the phosphate head
ATP hydrolysis phosphorylates the pump and changes its shape
A ribosome rotates the pump
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation powered by ATP hydrolysis drives the conformational change. Treating the pump as a passive channel ignores the ATP-dependent shape cycle.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hydrolysis of ATP phosphorylates the protein, triggering a shape change that exposes the Na⁺ binding sites to the extracellular space — where Na⁺ affinity drops, releasing the Na⁺ ions outside.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating the pump as a passive channel ignores the ATP-dependent shape cycle

questions.question: After releasing Na⁺ outside, what does the changed Na⁺/K⁺ pump bind?
options: Three intracellular K⁺ ions
Two extracellular Na⁺ ions
One ATP molecule only
Two extracellular K⁺ ions
questions.explanation: The outward-facing conformation binds two potassium ions from outside. Rebinding sodium at this stage prevents the required ion exchange.
questions.sourceEvidence: The changed shape now binds 2 K⁺ from outside.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Rebinding sodium at this stage prevents the required ion exchange

questions.question: What event returns the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to its original conformation?
options: Dephosphorylation
DNA replication
Neurotransmitter exocytosis
Osmotic lysis
questions.explanation: Removal of the phosphate restores the inward-facing shape and releases K⁺ inside. Assuming ATP remains attached throughout the cycle misses the phosphorylation switch.
questions.sourceEvidence: Dephosphorylation returns the protein to its original shape, releasing K⁺ inside the cell.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming ATP remains attached throughout the cycle misses the phosphorylation switch

questions.question: Three complete Na⁺/K⁺ pump cycles consume how many ATP molecules?
options: 1 ATP molecule
3 ATP molecules
2 ATP molecules
6 ATP molecules
questions.explanation: Each pump cycle consumes one ATP, so three cycles consume three ATP. Multiplying ATP use by the five transported ions overcounts the energy requirement.
questions.sourceEvidence: The net result: 3 Na⁺ pumped out, 2 K⁺ pumped in, 1 ATP consumed.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Multiplying ATP use by the five transported ions overcounts the energy requirement

questions.question: What is the ion total after two Na⁺/K⁺ pump cycles?
options: 4 Na⁺ out and 6 K⁺ in
6 Na⁺ in and 4 K⁺ out
6 Na⁺ out and 4 K⁺ in
2 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
questions.explanation: Doubling the three-to-two stoichiometry gives six sodium ions out and four potassium ions in. Reversing or equalizing the ion counts ignores the pump’s fixed exchange ratio.
questions.sourceEvidence: The net result: 3 Na⁺ pumped out, 2 K⁺ pumped in, 1 ATP consumed.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing or equalizing the ion counts ignores the pump’s fixed exchange ratio

questions.question: A cell encloses a large particle in a membrane vesicle and brings it inside. Which process is this?
options: Exocytosis
Simple diffusion
Osmosis
Endocytosis
questions.explanation: Endocytosis imports large material by forming an inward vesicle. Calling inward vesicle transport exocytosis reverses the direction of bulk transport.
questions.sourceEvidence: Endocytosis brings large material into the cell, while exocytosis fuses vesicles with the membrane to release material outside.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling inward vesicle transport exocytosis reverses the direction of bulk transport

questions.question: Which substance is specifically moving when a question describes osmosis?
options: Water
A solute only
ATP
A membrane protein
questions.explanation: Osmosis names the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Using osmosis for solute movement confuses the moving substance.
questions.sourceEvidence: Remember that osmosis describes water movement only, not solute movement.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using osmosis for solute movement confuses the moving substance

questions.question: Water separates a low-solute solution from a high-solute solution across a suitable membrane. What is the net direction of osmosis?
options: From high solute concentration to low solute concentration
From low solute concentration to high solute concentration
Toward the side with fewer water molecules and fewer solutes simultaneously
There is never net water movement
questions.explanation: Water moves toward the side with the higher solute concentration. Following solute diffusion instead of water movement reverses the osmotic direction.
questions.sourceEvidence: Water moves from low solute concentration to high solute concentration through a selectively permeable membrane.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Following solute diffusion instead of water movement reverses the osmotic direction

questions.question: Why is transport through an ion channel sometimes still passive?
options: Any protein automatically makes transport active
The channel always hydrolyzes ATP
The ion moves down its gradient without energy input
The ion moves against its gradient
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses a protein but remains downhill and energy independent. Classifying transport by protein use alone ignores gradient direction and ATP requirement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Facilitated diffusion is still passive because substances move down their gradient, even though a protein helps them cross.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Classifying transport by protein use alone ignores gradient direction and ATP requirement

questions.question: Which observation is strongest evidence that a transporter performs active transport?
options: It allows water to move through an aquaporin
It lets oxygen diffuse into the cell
It carries an ion down its gradient
It moves a solute against its gradient using energy
questions.explanation: Movement against a gradient requires an energy-coupled active mechanism. Protein assistance alone does not prove that transport is active.
questions.sourceEvidence: Active transport moves substances against the gradient and requires energy.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Protein assistance alone does not prove that transport is active

questions.question: Which orientation of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump is correct?
options: Three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in
Three Na⁺ in and two K⁺ out
Two Na⁺ out and three K⁺ in
Equal numbers of both ions out
questions.explanation: The pump has a fixed three-sodium-out and two-potassium-in stoichiometry. Reversing the exchange would undermine the gradients maintained by the pump.
questions.sourceEvidence: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in, not the reverse.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the exchange would undermine the gradients maintained by the pump

questions.question: Why is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump called an antiporter?
options: It moves both ions in the same direction
It moves Na⁺ and K⁺ in opposite directions
It transports only one type of ion
It prevents every ion from crossing
questions.explanation: Antiport couples the movement of different substances in opposite directions. Calling it a symporter incorrectly sends sodium and potassium the same way.
questions.sourceEvidence: It is an antiporter because the ions move in opposite directions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling it a symporter incorrectly sends sodium and potassium the same way

questions.question: Which set correctly predicts animal-cell volume in three solutions?
options: Hypertonic lyses, hypotonic shrinks, isotonic doubles volume
All three solutions cause lysis
Hypertonic shrinks, hypotonic swells or lyses, isotonic has no net change
All three solutions produce no net change
questions.explanation: Tonicity determines the direction and net effect of osmotic water movement. Swapping hypertonic and hypotonic outcomes reverses the water gradient.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hypertonic solutions shrink animal cells, hypotonic solutions can cause lysis, and isotonic solutions cause no net volume change.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Swapping hypertonic and hypotonic outcomes reverses the water gradient

questions.question: How does cholesterol buffer membrane fluidity across temperature changes?
options: It rigidifies the membrane at every temperature
It removes phospholipids when cold
It converts the bilayer into a cell wall when warm
It increases fluidity when cold and restrains fluidity when warm
questions.explanation: Cholesterol prevents excessive rigidity at low temperature and excessive fluidity at high temperature. Assigning one unchanging effect to cholesterol misses its temperature-dependent buffering role.
questions.sourceEvidence: Cholesterol increases membrane fluidity at low temperature and restrains it at high temperature.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning one unchanging effect to cholesterol misses its temperature-dependent buffering role
